cards.heading: What makes an API RESTful
cards.body: REST APIs use HTTP between a client and a server. They're stateless (every request carries everything needed, including authentication), cacheable where appropriate, and use a uniform interface: resources identified by URIs and manipulated with standard methods.

cards.heading: CRUD and HTTP methods
cards.body: Create → POST. Read → GET. Update → PUT (replace the whole resource) or PATCH (change part of it). Delete → DELETE. PUT can also create a resource at a URI you already know.
cards.example:
GET    /api/v1/devices          list devices
POST   /api/v1/vlans            create a VLAN
PATCH  /api/v1/interfaces/Gi0%2F1  change one field
DELETE /api/v1/vlans/30         remove VLAN 30
cards.mnemonic:
Create is POST, like posting a new letter. Read is GET. Delete is DELETE.
Update has two: PUT replaces the whole thing, like putting on new clothes, and PATCH changes one part, like patching a hole.

cards.heading: Anatomy of a request
cards.body: A request has a method, a URI (scheme, host, path, optional ?query parameters), headers (Authorization, Content-Type, Accept) and, for POST/PUT/PATCH, a body, usually JSON. The path (/api/v1/vlans) identifies the resource; a ?key=value query string can filter it. Content-Type describes the body you're sending (such as application/json); Accept lists the formats you want back.
cards.example:
POST https://dnac.example.com/api/v1/vlans
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGci...
Content-Type: application/json

{"id": 30, "name": "VOICE"}

cards.heading: Response codes
cards.body: 2xx success (200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content), 3xx redirection, 4xx client errors (400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found), 5xx server errors (500 Internal Server Error). 401 Unauthorized means authentication is missing or invalid; 403 Forbidden means the server knows who you are and refuses anyway.
cards.mnemonic:
The first digit tells the story: 2 is all good, 3 is "go see" (redirect), 4 is your fault (client), 5 is our fault (server).
401 vs 403: 401 asks "who are you?" (log in). 403 says "I know who you are, and no."
201 Created means a new thing now exists, and 404 means nothing is there.

cards.heading: Authentication
cards.body: Basic authentication sends a username and password (base64, so only safe over HTTPS). Many APIs exchange credentials once for a token that later requests send in an 'Authorization: Bearer' header. Others use an API key or OAuth. Catalyst Center, for example, returns a token that later requests send in an X-Auth-Token header.

cards.heading: Data formats
cards.body: JSON is the most common. XML (tags, used by NETCONF) and YAML (indentation-based, used by Ansible) carry the same kinds of data.
